title: Houston Mayor Curtails Police Cooperation With ICE — and Laredo Is Watching the Same Law
excerpt: Houston Mayor John Whitmire signed an executive order Friday barring police from alerting federal immigration officers over civil warrants during routine…
content:
Houston Mayor John Whitmire signed an executive order on Friday, Nov. 6, directing Houston police to curtail cooperation with federal immigration officers, a move he said he hopes becomes a model for other Texas cities, according to Reuters.

Under the new policy, officers on routine traffic stops or other detentions are barred from alerting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement solely on the basis of a civil immigration warrant against a person, according to Reuters. Police may notify ICE only if the person is also being arrested and charged with a jailable offense.

Whitmire said he acted after consulting the state's newly elected governor, lieutenant governor and comptroller, to "reduce fear and anxiety," and because "elections matter," according to Reuters. "I do this to begin a healing process," he said.

Houston Police Chief J. Noe Diaz joined Whitmire at the press conference, supported the change, and said the department had already begun implementing it, according to Reuters. The order took effect immediately, and it does not stop ICE from operating independently in Houston or bar contact after an arrest for a jailable offense, according to USA Today.

The state-law fight behind it

The order is a direct test of Texas's 2017 statute banning so-called "sanctuary city" policies, known as SB 4. Whitmire, a Democrat, voted against SB 4 as a state senator. He now says the order enforces SB 4 in line with its supporters' stated goal of targeting criminals in the country illegally, according to Reuters.

The backdrop is political. Gov. Greg Abbott, who lost his bid for a fourth term to Democrat Gina Hinojosa on Tuesday, Nov. 3, had threatened to withhold at least $110 million in public safety grants when Houston's council sought a similar ordinance months earlier, and city officials retreated at the time, according to Reuters and USA Today. Whether Abbott or the lame-duck state government will move to cut Houston's funding in response to the new order has not yet been reported.

What it means for Laredo

Laredo is a border city where local police and ICE cooperation, SB 4, and traffic-stop encounters with federal immigration enforcement are daily realities. The same state law governs Laredo police, and any local debate over the same question would now cite Houston's order as a reference point.

But no Laredo official has reacted publicly yet, and this story should not be read as a sign Laredo will follow suit. Webb Watch 956 will ask the City of Laredo and the Laredo Police Department whether Houston's move changes anything locally, and will report their answers.
